lessons.title: Building from the back
lessons.objective: You can explain build-up and playing out from the back.

payload.prompt: What is build-up play?

options.text: Scoring early in the match to get confidence
Moving the ball patiently from the goalkeeper through the thirds to create a shot
Stretching the pitch by shouting at your teammates

explanation.correct: Exactly. Build-up is how a team moves the ball from the back safely and methodically to create a chance.
explanation.incorrect: Build-up is patient ball movement from the goalkeeper and defenders through midfield to reach the attacking third.
explanation.sayThisLine: They build up patiently from the back, no panic.

payload.prompt: Playing out from the back means short passes from defence instead of long clearances. Why is it risky?

options.text: The goalkeeper is never ready for a pass
A misdirected pass near goal can turn into a chance for the opponent
Defenders get more tired from passing

explanation.correct: Right. Playing out draws the opponent higher, so an error can be punished quickly. But it also pulls them out of position.
explanation.incorrect: Playing out is risky because a turnover near your own goal gives the opponent an easy chance.
explanation.sayThisLine: Risky to play out from the back but when it works it's beautiful.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We need to build from the back, work the ball through the thirds.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Move the ball carefully and methodically towards the opponent's goal
Keep the ball for the full three thirds (defensive, middle, attacking)
Make three short passes then shoot
Use three players to build an attack

payload.translation: She means: don't rush or panic; move the ball safely through all the areas of the pitch until you reach the attacking third and can create a chance.

followUps.line: How many passes does a good build-up usually take?
followUps.why: Invites thinking about patience vs speed.

followUps.line: What happens if the build-up breaks down?
followUps.why: Asks about the risk he mentioned.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you're not sure, ask what part of the pitch they start from and where they want to end up.

payload.prompt: Playing out from the back draws the opponent forward. Why is that good for the team building out?

options.text: It gives them more room to run
It creates gaps the attackers can exploit
It tires out the opponents

explanation.correct: Correct. When defenders press high to stop the build-up, it creates space behind them and in the middle for your attackers.
explanation.incorrect: Playing out pulls the opponent forward and out of their organized shape, leaving gaps your attack can use.
explanation.sayThisLine: They came out to press, so the space opened up.

payload.prompt: Keeper under pressure plays short to a marked defender. Risky?

scene.alt: Goalkeeper with the ball in his box, an attacker nearby, passes to a defender who is being closed down.

explanation.correct: Yes. A turnover in your own box is dangerous. Playing out works best when you have time and space.
explanation.incorrect: Playing out under heavy pressure in your own box is a high-risk play that can lead to a quick goal against.
explanation.sayThisLine: Playing out is good but not when everyone is on you.

lessons.title: Progressive passes and through balls
lessons.objective: You can tell progressive passes and through balls apart.

payload.prompt: Match the pass type to what it does.

pairs.definition: A pass that moves the ball meaningfully closer to the opponent's goal.
A pass into the space behind the defence for a runner to chase.
A long pass from one flank to the other to attack the weak side.

explanation.summary: Progressive = forward and closer. Through ball = behind the line. Switch = across the pitch.
explanation.sayThisLine: He played a lovely through ball, split the defence.

payload.prompt: A midfielder passes forward 15 yards. It's not behind the defence, just a solid forward pass. Is that progressive?

options.text: Only if the receiver scores from it
Yes, moving the ball forward and closer to goal is progressive
No, only long passes are progressive

explanation.correct: Right. Progressive doesn't mean spectacular; it just means moving meaningfully forward.
explanation.incorrect: A progressive pass is any pass that moves the ball closer to the opponent's goal, not just long balls or through balls.
explanation.sayThisLine: He plays progressive passes, always looking forward.

payload.prompt: The midfielder plays a 20-yard pass into the space between the defender and goalkeeper. The striker runs onto it. Through ball?

scene.alt: Midfielder in possession, a gap between the last defender and the goal line, striker running forward into that space.

explanation.correct: Yes. A pass into the space behind the defence for a teammate to run onto is exactly a through ball.
explanation.incorrect: A through ball is designed to go behind the defence into space for a teammate to chase and attack.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lovely through ball, he split the whole line.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: Their xA is high but their progressive-pass count is low.

payload.question: What's she saying?

options.text: They create chances but don't move the ball forward effectively
They create chances from few forward passes, so they are efficient
Progressive passes are more important than creating chances
They don't play long balls

payload.translation: High xA (expected assists) means they set up good chances. Low progressive-pass count means they don't move the ball forward very often—so when they do, it counts.

followUps.line: How is that possible if they don't pass forward much?
Does that sound like a pressing team?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask her to explain which stat matters more: creating chances or progressing the ball.

payload.prompt: A typical attack sequence: defender to midfielder (progressive), midfielder to winger (progressive), winger to striker into space (through ball). Why does the final pass need to be a through ball?

options.text: Because the striker is too far away
Because the defence has reformed and is between the winger and striker
Because the striker is tired and needs rest

explanation.correct: Exactly. After moving the ball forward, the defence has shifted. A through ball into the space gets behind them.
explanation.incorrect: By the time you've built to the final pass, the defence has moved. A through ball bypasses them into the space where the striker can be one-on-one with the keeper.
explanation.sayThisLine: Progressive passes move the ball, through balls finish it off.

lessons.title: Find the overload (sim)
lessons.objective: You can find the free man by spotting the overload.

payload.prompt: Your team has three players in one zone and the opponent has two defenders there. What do you call that?

options.text: A triangle
An overload
A compact shape

explanation.correct: Right. An overload is having more players than the opponent in one area, which creates a free man.
explanation.incorrect: An overload means you have put more players than the defender into one zone, so someone is free.
explanation.sayThisLine: We overloaded the left and the right winger was free on the switch.

payload.prompt: Match the attacking concept.

pairs.definition: More attackers than defenders in one zone
A long pass from one flank to the weak-side attackers
A pass that sets up a pass to a third player running into space

explanation.summary: Overload = numbers advantage. Switch = flank to flank. Third-man run = sequence of two passes.
explanation.sayThisLine: That third-man run beat the whole line.

payload.prompt: Your team has four attackers in the box and the opponent has four defenders. Is anyone free?

scene.alt: Four attacking players versus four defending players in the penalty area.

explanation.correct: Correct. Equal numbers means everyone is marked. You need more attackers than defenders to have a free player.
explanation.incorrect: For a free man you need an overload: more attackers than the defenders marking them.
explanation.sayThisLine: You need numbers to create space.

statement.speaker: Manager
statement.text: They overloaded the left so hard the whole right side opened up.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The opponent pushed players to the left, leaving the right weak
They scored many goals on the left side
The left side was exhausted
The opponent's left defender was injured

payload.translation: The team sent so many players to attack the left side that the opponent's right side became empty. When the ball switched to the right, there was no one there to defend.

followUps.line: How did they score on the right if they overloaded the left?
Would that work against a team that shifts quickly?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unclear, ask him which side became empty and how the ball got there.

lessons.title: Crosses, cutbacks and overlaps
lessons.objective: You can explain crosses, cutbacks, overlaps and underlaps.

payload.prompt: Match the wide-play term.

pairs.definition: A ball from the wing into the box aimed at headers or tap-ins
A low pass from near the byline back towards the edge of the box
A teammate runs outside the ball carrier to give options
A teammate runs inside the ball carrier to give options

explanation.summary: Crosses go in; cutbacks go back. Overlap is outside; underlap is inside.
explanation.sayThisLine: The full-back overlapped and the winger went inside.

payload.prompt: A winger gets to the byline with the ball. Why might a cutback be better than a cross?

options.text: It's harder to score from a header than a tap-in
A low pass beats the goalkeeper's line better than a high ball
Cutbacks are always more accurate

explanation.correct: Right. A cutback is a low pass from the byline backwards into the box. It arrives at the striker's feet rather than making him jump.
explanation.incorrect: A cutback is a low pass from near the byline back towards the edge of the box. It bypasses the goalkeeper and the defender on the line.
explanation.sayThisLine: The cutback was better than the cross because it beats the keeper's line.

payload.prompt: The winger has the ball on the right wing. The right-back runs wide and forward outside him. Overlap?

scene.alt: Winger with the ball, a defender or fullback running to the outside edge of the winger.

explanation.correct: Yes. The full-back running outside (to the right of) the winger is an overlap—he gives the winger another option.
explanation.incorrect: An overlap is when a teammate runs outside the ball carrier to provide an option and pull defenders away.
explanation.sayThisLine: The right-back overlapped and the winger went inside.

payload.prompt: Why do overlaps and underlaps work as attacking tactics?

options.text: They confuse the defence by giving multiple passing options
They force the defender to make a choice and one option is always free
They tire the defenders by making them run

explanation.correct: Exactly. When a defender is marked by two options (the ball carrier and the runner), he can only stop one, so one is always free.
explanation.incorrect: Overlaps and underlaps work because they create an overload: the defender marking the winger now has to decide, and one of the two is free.
explanation.sayThisLine: The overlap gave him options and one was always free.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: A winger dribbled back from the byline towards the edge of the box and passed
A winger crossed the ball from the wing
The goalkeeper caught a high pass
The winger cut the ball in half

payload.translation: The winger got to the very edge of the pitch (byline) and passed backwards, low and across the box, for a teammate to tap in.

followUps.line: Why didn't he just cross it?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask him where the winger was when he made the pass and what direction it went.

lessons.title: Pressing triggers (sim)
lessons.objective: You can recognise a pressing trigger and call the press.

payload.prompt: What is a pressing trigger?

options.text: The whistle that starts a match
A cue that tells the team to press together, like a back pass or a bad touch
A foul that results in a yellow card

explanation.correct: Right. A trigger is a moment when the team recognises it's time to press: a back pass, a poor first touch, a pass to the wing.
explanation.incorrect: A pressing trigger is a cue—usually a bad pass or touch—that signals the whole team to close down the opponent immediately.
explanation.sayThisLine: The back pass was the trigger and they all went.

payload.prompt: Match the pressing style.

pairs.definition: Closing down an opponent quickly to win the ball or force a bad pass
Pressing in the opponent's half to win the ball close to goal
A cue like a back pass that signals the whole team to press

explanation.summary: Pressing is the tactic; high press is where; trigger is when.
explanation.sayThisLine: They press like mad, high up the pitch.

payload.prompt: The goalkeeper is on the ball with time and space, moving it forward. Is this a pressing trigger?

scene.alt: Goalkeeper with the ball in his hands, calm, with no opponent nearby.

explanation.correct: No. A pressing trigger is a moment of weakness: a bad touch, a back pass, or being under pressure. This is a calm goalkeeper.
explanation.incorrect: A pressing trigger is a moment when the opponent has a problem: a poor touch, a back pass to the keeper, or being closed down. A calm goalkeeper is not a trigger.
explanation.sayThisLine: Press on the back pass, not on the keeper in open space.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: They pressed like mad, won it high and scored in six seconds.

payload.question: What's she describing?

options.text: A high press that worked perfectly
A defensive foul that led to a goal
A counterattack from a goal kick
A very fast player

payload.translation: They used aggressive high pressing to win the ball near the opponent's goal, and because the opponent was out of shape, they scored almost immediately.

followUps.line: Why is six seconds so fast for a goal after winning it?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of shape and positioning.

followUps.line: What happens if the press doesn't work?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask her which team's goal they scored and what they did with the ball.

lessons.title: High press, mid-block, low block
lessons.objective: You can tell the three defensive blocks apart.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive block to where and how it works.

pairs.definition: Win the ball high, close to the opponent's goal
Sit in the middle third and press when the ball enters your zone
Defend deep and compact, hit on the counter

explanation.summary: High = close to goal. Mid = in the middle. Low = deep and compact.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're a low block who counter-press when they lose it high.

payload.prompt: A team plays with their back line on the halfway line, closing down the opponent in midfield. What block is that?

options.text: High press
Mid-block
Low block

explanation.correct: Right. Mid-block: they sit in the middle third and press when it comes into their zone.
explanation.incorrect: That's a mid-block. High press is even higher, in the opponent's half. Low block is much deeper.
explanation.sayThisLine: We sat in a mid-block and waited.

payload.prompt: A low-block team parks the bus and defends deep. What is the main way to score against them?

options.text: Lots of short passes
A quick counter after winning the ball
Patient build-up play until they break

explanation.correct: Exactly. A low block invites pressure. You have to be patient and work the ball until they break or a gap opens.
explanation.incorrect: Against a low block, they're compact and organized, so a quick counter won't work. You need to break them down with build-up play.
explanation.sayThisLine: They parked the bus and nicked one on the break.

payload.prompt: Your team's back line is in the opponent's half, pressing the opponent's midfielder on the ball. High press?

scene.alt: Defending players standing in the attacking third, close to an opponent with the ball.

explanation.correct: Yes. Playing in the opponent's half and pressing there is a high press.
explanation.incorrect: A high press means defending high up the pitch, in the opponent's half, close to their goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: High press, and they scored within six seconds of winning it.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: They set a low block to frustrate our build-up.

payload.question: What's the strategy?

options.text: Defend high to stop the build-up before it starts
Defend deep and compact to force us to work hard for a chance
Press immediately after losing the ball
Defend in the middle of the pitch

payload.translation: They're playing defensively deep, staying organized in the box, making it hard for you to build an attack and break them down.

followUps.line: How do you break down a low block?
Why would they frustrate the build-up if they're defending deep?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of patience vs mistakes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask where their defenders are standing and what they're trying to prevent.

lessons.title: Line height (sim)
lessons.objective: You can explain how a high line squeezes space and risks the ball over the top.

payload.prompt: A team holds a high defensive line, with centre-backs near the halfway line. What is the advantage?

options.text: More space in front of the goalkeeper to recover
Squeezes the opponent's attacking space and keeps them offside
Keeps the full-backs from overlapping

explanation.correct: Right. A high line squeezes the space available to attackers and makes it harder to play the ball in behind.
explanation.incorrect: A high line compresses the pitch, leaving less space for the opponent in the attacking third and catching strikers in offside positions.
explanation.sayThisLine: They hold a really high line, so one ball over the top hurts.

payload.prompt: What is the risk of playing a high line?

options.text: The goalkeeper gets tired from distributing the ball
One ball over the top puts an attacker free with a clear run to goal
Offside is harder to call

explanation.correct: Exactly. If the high line is breached, there's a lot of space between the defenders and the goalkeeper.
explanation.incorrect: Playing high leaves room behind the line. A long ball over the top exploits this space and the attacker is one-on-one.
explanation.sayThisLine: That long ball was perfect, acres of space behind the line.

payload.prompt: A team holds a high line with their back four near the opponent's box. The goalkeeper is 40 yards behind them. Good defensive shape?

scene.alt: Defenders standing high up the pitch, far from their own goalkeeper.

explanation.correct: Risky. That's too much space between the line and the keeper. If the line breaks, it's a one-on-one.
explanation.incorrect: A high line is good for squeezing space, but if it's too high with too much gap to the keeper, a through ball is lethal.
explanation.sayThisLine: They hold a high line but there's too much space to the keeper.

statement.speaker: Manager
statement.text: Our high line worked, they were all offside today.

payload.question: What's she saying?

options.text: Her team's high line caught attackers in offside positions
All the opposition's goals were ruled offside
Her team scored while offside
The referee didn't understand the offside rule

payload.translation: By playing a high defensive line, she kept the opponent's strikers in offside positions throughout the match. They couldn't attack because they were always behind the line.

followUps.line: What happens if the line drops too deep?
Did the high line let your team control the ball?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask her what she means by 'they were all offside'—does it mean they were called offside, or they couldn't get onside?

lessons.title: Counter-press and counterattack
lessons.objective: You can explain the five seconds after losing the ball.

payload.prompt: What is a counter-press?

options.text: Pressing the opponent after your team loses the ball
Pressing during a throw-in
A foul that leads to a press

explanation.correct: Right. A counter-press is immediate pressing after losing the ball to win it back before the opponent organises.
explanation.incorrect: A counter-press means pressing immediately after losing possession, trying to regain it quickly while the opponent is still out of shape.
explanation.sayThisLine: Counter-press, they won it back in five seconds.

payload.prompt: Match the transition concept.

pairs.definition: Pressing immediately after losing the ball
A fast attack after winning the ball while the opponent is out of shape
Players staying back to stop the counterattack

explanation.summary: Counter-press = win it back fast. Counterattack = score fast. Rest defence = cover for attacks.
explanation.sayThisLine: Great rest defence, he was back to snuff it out.

payload.prompt: Your team wins the ball in your own half. The opponent still has three defenders back, but your attackers are already moving forward. Is this a good moment to counterattack?

scene.alt: Your team with the ball in their own half, several defenders retreating.

explanation.correct: Yes. If your attackers are moving and the opponent's defence is still high, it's a perfect time to hit them on the break.
explanation.incorrect: A counterattack works when the opponent is out of shape and your attackers are already moving. Three defenders back might not be enough.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lightning counter, three passes and it was in the net.

payload.scenario: Your team wins the ball on the left side. Three attackers are racing forward. Do you (A) join the attack to make it 4v3, or (B) stay back to cover for a counter?

options.text: Join the attack, push numbers forward
options.reason: You'd be 4v3 going forward, more chance to score.

options.text: Stay back and cover
options.reason: If they break your attack, they'd be on you with space.

explanation.correct: Smart. Counterattacks are dangerous because if you lose the ball high, they have space. Always have rest defence.
explanation.incorrect: If all four push forward and lose the ball, their three attackers have a free run. Rest defence means leaving one player back.
explanation.sayThisLine: You need rest defence for a counterattack.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We lost the ball but we counter-pressed and scored from the counter in six seconds.

payload.question: What happened?

options.text: They won the ball back immediately and scored from a fast break
They fouled the opponent and scored from a free kick
They let the opponent attack and defended well
They had two forwards at halftime

payload.translation: After losing the ball, they pressed immediately (counter-press) to win it back in the opponent's half, then attacked fast (counterattack) before the opponent could reorganise. All in six seconds.

followUps.line: Why is the counter-press so important for a counterattack?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask him which team had the ball first and last.

lessons.title: Zonal, man and tempo
lessons.objective: You can explain zonal vs man marking and tempo.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept.

pairs.definition: Defenders guard areas of the pitch, not specific opponents
Defenders follow a specific opponent everywhere
Speeding up or slowing the game deliberately

explanation.summary: Zonal = areas. Man = players. Tempo = pace.
explanation.sayThisLine: Are they zonal or man-marking at corners?

payload.prompt: A defender marks a zone. An opponent moves into it. Does the defender stay with the zone or follow the player?

options.text: Stays with the zone and hands off to a teammate
Follows the player out of the zone
Fouls the player to stop him

explanation.correct: Right. In zonal marking, when an opponent leaves your zone, you hand him off to the defender in the next zone.
explanation.incorrect: Zonal defenders guard areas, not players. When an opponent leaves, the next zone's defender takes him.
explanation.sayThisLine: They switched to hybrid marking after conceding three corner goals.

payload.prompt: Your team is winning 1-0. Do you speed up the game or slow it down?

scene.alt: A team leading by one goal near the end of the match.

explanation.correct: Slow it down. Less time means less chance for the opponent to equalise.
explanation.incorrect: When you're winning, slow the game down. More time on the clock = more chances for the opponent to score.
explanation.sayThisLine: They had 70 percent possession but no control.

payload.prompt: A team has 65% possession but 'no control'. What might that mean?

options.text: They pass fast but the opponent intercepts most passes
They have the ball but can't dictate the pace or shape of the game
The goalkeeper is nervous

explanation.correct: Right. Possession is not the same as control. Control means dictating the pace and rhythm.
explanation.incorrect: Possession is having the ball; control is using it to dictate how the game flows and what you want to happen.
explanation.sayThisLine: They had 70 percent possession but no control.

statement.speaker: Defender
statement.text: At corners they're zonal so there are gaps between us. We go man-to-man.

payload.question: What's he saying?

options.text: The opponent defends zones, so his team follows individual players instead
His team plays zonal defence all the time
Man-to-man is better than zonal
There are gaps in the corner flag

payload.translation: The opponent uses zonal marking at corners (everyone guards an area), which creates gaps between zones. So his team switches to man-to-man (following specific players), which covers the gaps.

followUps.line: Why do the zones create gaps?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask him which system covers gaps and which leaves them.
